summary: Describes a protocol that supports 3270 devices more fully than existing tn3270 practice. It is a standards-track proposal. It was replaced by RFC 2355.

plainLanguage.summary: A better way to use old mainframe terminals over a network. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how do tn3270e clients request device names
how does tn3270e support the attn key
subtitle: Better support for IBM 3270 terminals and printers over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Traditional tn3270 support for 3270 terminals over Telnet lacks features like printer emulation, device naming, and response handling.
tldr.mechanism: TN3270E adds a new Telnet option with device-type negotiation, function negotiation, and a message header system to enable full 3270 and printer emulation.
tldr.outcome: Provides richer terminal and printer emulation capabilities over Telnet, including support for SNA responses and special keys like ATTN and SYSREQ. Replaced by RFC 2355.

today: RFC 1647 was a Proposed Standard published in July 1994 and was replaced by RFC 2355. It is no longer the recommended way to emulate 3270 terminals over Telnet, though the protocol remains historically significant for understanding legacy terminal emulation.

sections.title: Introduction and Limitations of Traditional tn3270
sections.content:
Traditional tn3270 is the existing practice of emulating 3270 terminals over Telnet by negotiating three Telnet options: Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission, and End of Record. While functional, this approach has several significant shortcomings that limit its use.

The primary limitations are: no support for 3270 printer emulation, no mechanism for clients to request a specific device-name (crucial for host applications that expect a particular terminal identity), limited support for the ATTN and SYSREQ keys, no support for SNA positive and negative responses (essential for printer operation), and no way for clients to access SNA Bind information.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of using mainframe terminals over Telnet works, but it is missing important features like printing and special keyboard keys that mainframes need.

sections.title: TN3270E Overview and Core Features
sections.content:
TN3270E is a new Telnet option (option code 40) that addresses these limitations. It allows clients and servers to negotiate whether to use TN3270E or fall back to traditional tn3270 if either side does not support it.

The protocol has two major negotiation phases. First, device-type negotiation determines what kind of device the client will emulate. Supported types include terminal devices like IBM-3278-2 (24x80 display) through IBM-3278-5-E (27x132 with extended features), and the IBM-3287-1 printer. Second, function negotiation determines which optional 3270 functions both sides support, such as SCS control codes (for printers), data stream control, response handling, Bind image passing, and SYSREQ key emulation.
sections.plainLanguage: TN3270E lets the computer and the terminal agree on what type of device it is—a terminal or printer—and what special features they both support before they start talking.

sections.title: Message Header and Data Structure
sections.content:
Each 3270 data message in TN3270E is prefixed with a 5-byte header containing four fields: DATA-TYPE (1 byte) indicates the type of data following the header, such as 3270-DATA, SCS-DATA, RESPONSE, BIND-IMAGE, or NVT-DATA. REQUEST-FLAG (1 byte) is only meaningful for REQUEST type messages and indicates when printer error conditions have been cleared. RESPONSE-FLAG (1 byte) indicates whether the sender expects a response and whether a response (positive or negative) was sent. SEQ-NUMBER (2 bytes) correlates responses to requests when the RESPONSES function has been negotiated.

The message format is: <TN3270E Header><data><IAC EOR>. For certain message types without a data portion, the header is immediately followed by the end-of-record marker.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a small label that says what kind of message it is, whether we are expecting an answer back, and a number to keep track of questions and answers.

sections.title: Device Pools and Connection Types
sections.content:
TN3270E servers maintain organized pools of device-names from which they assign identities to connecting clients. The generic terminal pool provides any available terminal for clients that do not request a specific device-name. A separate specific terminal pool contains named terminals that clients might request explicitly via the CONNECT command. The server may also maintain paired printer devices, where each terminal has an associated printer that can be requested via the ASSOCIATE command. Independent printer pools provide devices for printers that are not paired with terminals.

The DEVICE-TYPE negotiation uses REQUEST commands (sent by the client) and IS commands (sent by the server to accept) or REJECT commands (with reason codes like DEVICE-IN-USE or INV-DEVICE-NAME) to resolve device assignments. Multiple negotiation rounds may be needed if the client must try different device-names.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps lists of available terminals and printers. When a client connects, it can ask for a specific one or let the server pick one. The server says yes or explains why not.

sections.title: Special Functions and Key Support
sections.content:
TN3270E supports several specialized functions beyond basic data transfer. The RESPONSES function lets the server reflect positive and negative response requirements from the host application, enabling printer sessions to indicate success, error conditions (such as "printer not ready"), or device status issues.

The ATTN key is supported by mapping a client key to the Telnet Interrupt Process (IP) command, which the server translates into an SNA SIGNAL RU for SNA environments. The SYSREQ key is implemented using the Telnet Abort Output (AO) command and enters a "suspended mode" where the client can communicate directly with the host SSCP (System Services Control Point) to issue commands like LOGOFF. The BIND-IMAGE function passes the SNA session bind information to the client and notifies it when SNA sessions begin and end via UNBIND messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Special keys and features let the terminal do things like interrupt the host, ask the mainframe directly for help, or tell the terminal about the active session.
